title: Make your first contribution
summary: Find a project, get a reproducible build, and send a useful change.

sections.title: Start with the project's own instructions
sections.text: Choose a game you care about and open its repository. Read the README, contribution guide, open issues, and existing pull requests. Decomp Atlas helps you find projects; the upstream maintainers decide what work is useful and what they will merge.

sections.title: Build before changing anything
sections.text: Use the exact game version, compiler, and setup steps required upstream. Supply any original files from your own authorized copy; this catalogue does not distribute game binaries. Confirm the unmodified project builds before trying to match a function.

sections.title: Choose a small piece of work
sections.text: Look for a documented task, a function the maintainers want matched, or a documentation fix. Check existing claims and ask in the upstream issue or community channel before duplicating someone else's work. A progress tile describes a unit of code; it is not automatically an available task.

sections.title: Compare, explain, and open a pull request
sections.text: Run the upstream checks and comparison tools. Keep your change focused, explain what changed, and include the validation the project requests. Retain author credits and respond to review. For example, Ocarina of Time welcomes small contributions and points readers to its community for support; Pokémon Emerald has a pull request checklist.

title: Set up a decomp.dev progress board
summary: Turn an upstream build report into a browsable map of translation units.

sections.title: What a board actually shows
sections.text: objdiff compares objects produced from reconstructed source with reference objects. A unit is usually a translation unit, such as one source file. Function views help contributors investigate differences. Fuzzy similarity, fully matched code, and completed or linked code are distinct measurements. Check each dashboard's labels and version before interpreting a percentage.

sections.title: Prepare a reproducible comparison
sections.text: Follow the official integration guide to configure objdiff.json, including expected target objects and objects built from source. Keep the object paths and version identifiers consistent with the build. The exact setup depends on your repository; copying another game's paths will not configure yours.

sections.title: Generate and upload a report
sections.text: Once the comparison is configured and the build succeeds, generate a report with objdiff-cli. In GitHub Actions, upload the report as an artifact named VERSION_report, replacing VERSION with the actual version identifier. Keep copyrighted reference binaries out of the public artifact.

sections.title: Register the project
sections.text: Get a successful report-producing workflow onto the repository's default branch. A repository administrator can then add the project at decomp.dev/manage/new. The decomp.dev GitHub App supports workflow notifications and configurable pull request comments. Follow the official guide for current installation and artifact settings.

sections.title: Link the board and its units
sections.text: Add the board URL to your README and your Atlas listing. You can link a specific unit using the URL generated by the board; the Sims 2 reference uses ?unit=targets_s2c. If a board is disabled or a build stops uploading, tell readers and keep the last report's date visible. Do not treat a historical report as live progress.

title: Get a repository listed
summary: Open a submission ticket or contribute a listing through a pull request.

sections.title: Gather the original sources
sections.text: Find the canonical repository, project title, target platform, maintainer or team credit, and contribution instructions. Include a progress board if the project has one. A listing can be useful without a board; an unverified percentage is not required.

sections.title: Open a submission ticket
sections.text: Use Submit a repo to prepare your ticket. Review its contents, then open it on GitHub and submit it there. Preparing a ticket on this site does not publish it. A maintainer checks the source, duplicate listings, credits, and links before accepting it.

sections.title: Or send a pull request
sections.text: Fork the Atlas repository, add one entry to data/projects.json using the existing fields, and run npm run build followed by npm run check. Include upstream sources in the pull request. Keep progress outside the catalogue unless a dated, attributable measurement is explicitly supported.

sections.title: Keep the record useful
sections.text: Report a moved repository, incorrect credit, broken board, or outdated contribution link using a correction ticket. Catalogue edits and wiki improvements go through the same review process. Listings do not imply that the original maintainers endorse Atlas.

title: Credit people. Label the numbers.
summary: How the catalogue attributes projects and avoids misleading progress claims.

sections.title: The project belongs to its creators
sections.text: Every listing identifies the upstream maintainer or team and links to its canonical repository. Atlas is a discovery and learning site by Owen. Listed projects, their code, names, and assets remain under their respective owners' rights and terms. A listing is not a claim of authorship, partnership, or endorsement.

sections.title: Build success is one piece of evidence
sections.text: A working executable can still include original binary data or code. Sims2DECOMP explicitly distinguishes a byte-identical linked DOL from fully reconstructed source. Read the upstream methodology before interpreting a headline percentage.

sections.title: Live data needs a live source
sections.text: The catalogue is curated, bundled information and is labeled NON-LIVE DATA. External boards show their own measurements. This version does not fetch progress or contributor counts, so it does not invent them. A board can be stale or disabled even when its page still shows numbers.

sections.title: Correct a credit or source
sections.text: Open a correction ticket with the listing URL, the proposed correction, and an authoritative source. Credit corrections receive the same review as new listings. Use the upstream project's own channel for questions about its code or contribution decisions.
